claims.text: GeoDeploy pairs TypeSafe Jev's confidence-scored decisions with the Pulumi Automation API to place and scale Kubernetes across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.
GeoDeploy is open source, released today (as of the post date), and picks the best AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud region for users, gating every AI decision on confidence.
GeoDeploy prices every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes.
GeoDeploy asks Jev to pick the best region per geo from a closed list, so Jev cannot hallucinate a region.
GeoDeploy gates every Jev decision on confidence, with hard rejects for data residency.
GeoDeploy provisions consistent Kubernetes clusters using one Pulumi stack per region.
In GeoDeploy's self-driving mode, the system scales itself, with a human in the loop when Jev's confidence is low.
TypeSafe AI opened early access to Jev, its SystemOne model, in the week before this post (published 2026-09-25).
Jev is TypeSafe AI's SystemOne model.
TypeSafe's Jev comes with a set of AI primitives that let apps, agents, and workflows make decisions based on context.
Jev's decision-making primitives are confidence scoring, multiple choice, and yes/no (noul) questions.
Jev's decision-making primitives are "the perfect complement to agentic work."
Combining Jev's reasoning with Pulumi means the gap between dreaming up ideal infrastructure and deploying it to production practically vanishes.
GeoDeploy compares every AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud region that offers managed Kubernetes, picks the best one for each geo, and provisions consistent environments across all three hyperscalers.
Jev never does arithmetic, generates code, or invents region names; it only selects from closed sets of region IDs that GeoDeploy has already priced and checked.
GeoDeploy fetches current AWS prices from the AWS Price List API.
GeoDeploy fetches current Azure prices from the Azure Retail Prices API.
GeoDeploy fetches current Google Cloud prices from the Google Cloud Billing Catalog, normalizing all three into a single quote format.
GeoDeploy's deterministic TypeScript bin-packs pods onto nodes, filters out instance types that don't match the image's architecture, and computes a monthly cost for each candidate region.

GeoDeploy assembles a Pulumi program from a curated registry of typed modules covering EKS, AKS, or GKE; ECR, ACR, or Artifact Registry; ingress; DNS through Route 53, NS1, or Cloudflare; and observability.
GeoDeploy's Pulumi Automation API step runs a preview and then an update, one stack per region, and refuses to run unless cloud credentials pass readiness checks.
The link /automation/ points to a Pulumi Automation API page that exists on the Pulumi website.
Every GeoDeploy run writes a `plan.json` and `plan.md` containing the full decision record, and a web UI shows the deployment on a live globe.
Jev doesn't return free text; it returns typed answers with calibrated confidence through three primitives.
Jev's `choice()` primitive picks one option from a closed list and returns the pick, a probability distribution across all options, and a confidence.
Jev's `score()` primitive rates something against a rubric the caller describes, and GeoDeploy uses 10 levels in its rubrics.
Jev's `noul()` primitive answers a yes/no question with a single probability.
Because Jev only selects from closed sets, a hallucinated region such as `us-west-9` or a made-up Pulumi argument cannot happen by construction in GeoDeploy.
For each geo, GeoDeploy sends Jev a shortlist of up to 40 priced candidates along with the constraints and the image's architecture.

In a single call, GeoDeploy asks Jev for a region selection (choice), five quality scores (score: coverage, cost fit, maturity, sprawl risk, architecture consistency), two hard checks (noul: data residency satisfied, enough capacity), and a fallback region (choice).
The file `packages/decide/src/questions.ts` in the GeoDeploy repo contains the `buildStageAQuestions` function that builds Jev's questions.
The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package exports `choice`, `noul`, and `score`.
The options passed to `choice()` are the priced candidates themselves, keyed by ID, so Jev cannot answer with a region that isn't on the list.
TypeSafe advises rubric authors to "describe situations, not degrees."

GeoDeploy's rubrics use 10 levels, each a concrete scenario, running from "Serves users on a different continent with no nearby presence" up to "In-geo with multiple availability zones, directly in or adjacent to the demand geo's primary population center."

The `@typesafe-ai/sdk` package exposes a `TypeSafeClient` class whose `systemOne({ state, questions })` method returns a result with an `answers` object, where each answer has fields such as `selection.choice`, `selection.confidence`, `residencyOk.noul`, and `coverage.score`.
GeoDeploy sends the whole question set to Jev in one call, along with the state Jev reasons over.
GeoDeploy's five scores feed a ranking system that runs on weight profiles: latency-optimized (the default), balanced, residency-first, and failure-domain.
Because GeoDeploy's ranking weights live in code, the ranking can be re-tuned without calling Jev again.
In GeoDeploy's composite ranking, sprawl risk is subtracted from the score while cost fit, coverage, maturity, and architecture consistency are added.
Every extra cloud provider means more credentials, tooling, and on-call runbooks.
In GeoDeploy, cluster and registry modules follow directly from the provider (AWS always means EKS and ECR), and Jev decides only ingress posture, autoscaling posture, and node-pool sizing tier.
GeoDeploy's data-residency confidence gate has a threshold of 0.95, and failing it causes a hard reject.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for choosing a region for a new cluster is 0.90; if it doesn't pass, the top three candidates are flagged for a human to choose.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for the region when a stack already exists is 0.75; if it doesn't pass, the existing region is kept.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for an ingress or autoscaling module choice is 0.85; if it doesn't pass, the registry default is used.
GeoDeploy's confidence threshold for the node-pool sizing tier is 0.60; if it doesn't pass, the bin-packing result is used.
GeoDeploy has a global confidence floor of 0.50 for region pick, residency, or capacity; if it doesn't pass, the AI path is dropped for that geo.
The residency check shown is from `packages/decide/src/engine.ts` in the GeoDeploy repo, and it is followed by a validation that the selection is one of the candidates.
Enforcing a confidence gate in GeoDeploy is plain deterministic code, not an AI decision.
Each `AiPathAborted` in GeoDeploy carries the full attempt (state, questions, and answers), so even a rejected answer ends up in the audit trail.

If a gate check fails, the Jev API times out or returns an error, or the upstream can't be reached, GeoDeploy switches to a deterministic fallback that compares prices across providers while still enforcing the residency and constraint checks.
The GeoDeploy command `geodeploy explain` shows why each region won.
GeoDeploy's self-driving mode is enabled with the `geodeploy monitor` command.

In self-driving mode, GeoDeploy periodically checks each deployment's CPU utilization and asks Jev one joint question across all regions with options `no-change`, `scale-up:<geo>`, `scale-down:<geo>`, or `shift:<from>-><to>`, plus a separate check on disruption risk.
In self-driving mode, code rather than Jev computes the actual node-count changes.
In self-driving mode, above 0.85 confidence the resize is applied automatically.
In self-driving mode, between 0.70 and 0.85 confidence the resize is suggested for a human to approve.
In self-driving mode, below 0.70 confidence GeoDeploy ignores Jev's pick and falls back to a deterministic per-region rule based on observed utilization.

CPU utilization alone makes a poor autoscaling metric; once a traffic baseline is established it is usually paired with other signals such as median end-to-end request latency, error rates, or something application-specific.
GeoDeploy is released as open source, and anyone with access to Jev and a cloud provider can get started today.
The GitHub repository github.com/pulumi/devx-geodeploy exists and contains GeoDeploy.
The Pulumi Automation API docs page exists at /docs/iac/automation-api/.
TypeSafe's Jev documentation introduction page exists at https://docs.typesafe.ai/introduction.
Pulumi's X account handle is @PulumiCorp, at https://x.com/PulumiCorp.
A free Pulumi account can be signed up for at https://app.pulumi.com/signup.
